title: Elodie and the Letters
premise: Wren Winterbourne keeps her late grandfather's lighthouse on the grey coast of Pellow Bay, writing romance novels under a pen name while refusing to live one. When a storm washes a mail sack ashore containing an eleven-year-old undelivered letter — addressed to her, from the boy who vanished the night her family's fishing boat sank — she is forced to reopen the tragedy that made her. The letter reveals her grandfather falsified the wreck report to protect someone, and as Wren and the letter's author, now a coast guard investigator named Jonah Vale, dig into what really happened, they uncover a cover-up that once saved a life at the cost of the truth. In the end, Wren must choose between exposing the lie that gives her found family its fragile peace and forgiving it, letting Jonah stay past the last train out of the harvest festival — because love, like light, only matters if you keep it burning for someone.
about_author: Silas Nystrom is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered letters in coastal postal dead-letter offices before turning to fiction. They write on the northern English coast, where every lighthouse has a story the keepers never told.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Establishes her solitary routine: tending the automated lighthouse, drafting her third novel, dodging the village's pity after eleven years since the sinking. Her grandfather's death left her the light and a locked desk drawer she's never opened. Emotional beat: comfortable numbness about to crack.

chapters.title: What the Sea Returns
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A winter storm strands a rusted mail sack on the tideline; inside, water-swollen but legible, a letter postmarked eleven years ago, addressed to Wren in handwriting she'd know anywhere — Jonah Vale's. She doesn't open it. Emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity; the past knocking politely.

chapters.title: Past Tense
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Wren's POV. Eleven years earlier: seventeen-year-old Wren and Jonah on the pier before the boat went down, his sudden departure, the funeral where he never appeared. Shows why she writes love only in the past tense. Emotional beat: first heartbreak rendered as origin wound.

chapters.title: The Reading
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She finally opens the letter: Jonah wrote that he saw something the night of the wreck, that he was leaving to protect her, and that if she's reading this, he failed to come back for her. The letter names no one — but mentions 'the second boat.' Emotional beat: grief reorganized into questions.

chapters.title: A Man Off the Last Train
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Coast guard investigator Jonah Vale arrives in Pellow Bay officially to review historical incident files, unofficially because the dead-letter office finally released his letter and he needs to know if Wren read it. He checks into the inn and learns the festival begins in three weeks. Emotional beat: guilt wearing a uniform.

chapters.title: The Second Boat
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren confronts the harbormaster's widow, Maren, who lets slip that two boats went out that night, not one — and that Wren's grandfather, the keeper, logged only one. Jonah witnesses the exchange. Emotional beat: the town's complicity surfacing like wreckage.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Tea
chapters.summary: Jonah and Wren's POV, alternating within scenes. Their first real conversation in eleven years is a careful duel: each knows the other knows something. She accuses him of abandoning her; he asks what her grandfather told her. Neither tells everything. Emotional beat: old intimacy weaponized, then regretted.

chapters.title: The Locked Drawer
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. She opens her grandfather's desk at last: the true logbook, pages cut out, and a photograph of the second boat's crew — including a teenage boy, Tam Osgood, whose father was the other skipper. A note in her grandfather's hand: 'He was only fourteen.' Emotional beat: the hero of her childhood becomes a mystery.

chapters.title: Found Family, Frayed
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. The village's surrogate family — Maren, the Osgoods, the festival committee who raised Wren after the funerals — gathers for festival prep, and Wren watches them with new eyes, wondering who cut the logbook and who kept the secret. Emotional beat: warmth shadowed by suspicion; loyalty tested by truth.

chapters.title: Tam
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah tracks down Tam Osgood, now a fisherman running his late father's boat. Tam admits his father took the second boat out that night to smuggle debt-ridden families' goods past customs — and that Wren's grandfather saw him, and let him go, and the fishing boat went down in the wake of the chase. Emotional beat: confession as burden-sharing.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Reeling, Wren reconstructs it: her grandfather falsified the report so Tam wouldn't be orphaned twice — by prison — but the lie also buried the truth that the wreck wasn't weather alone. She rages at the dead man who chose mercy over justice. Emotional beat: betrayal and understanding arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: Drafts and Confessions
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah confesses to Wren why he left: her grandfather begged him to stay silent until Tam came of age, and Jonah — an orphan himself, taken in by the same village — obeyed, choosing the boy over the girl. Wren throws him out. Emotional beat: the reunion collapses under the weight of old choices.

chapters.title: The Festival Opens
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, anchored by Wren. The lantern festival begins; the whole found family assembles, and Wren must smile through the opening ceremony beside people she now suspects of burying her parents' truth. Jonah watches from the crowd, uninvited. Emotional beat: public joy, private fracture.

chapters.title: Maren's Night
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren, drunk on festival cider, reveals she was the one who mailed Jonah's letter years ago and let it 'go missing' — she'd promised Wren's grandfather to protect the secret until it could do no harm. She begs Wren to let the dead rest. Emotional beat: the keeper of secrets becomes their confessor.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: Wren and Jonah's POV. Wren faces the choice: report the falsified log and the smuggling (destroying Tam's livelihood and the village's peace), or honor her grandfather's mercy. Jonah offers a third path — the truth told on their terms, to the family first. Emotional beat: justice reframed as repair, not punishment.

chapters.title: The Telling
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Wren gathers Maren, Tam, and the Osgoods in the lighthouse and reads her grandfather's hidden pages aloud: the whole night, the whole choice. Silence, anger, Tam's tears, Maren's relief. The family does not break — it bends. Emotional beat: catharsis; the secret loses its power by being spoken.

chapters.title: What Tam Owes
chapters.summary: Tam's POV. Tam chooses to make restitution outside the law: funding a memorial for the lost crew and restoring the lighthouse, publicly framed as gratitude, privately as penance. Some villagers suspect; none press. Emotional beat: survival's debt acknowledged without a courtroom.

chapters.title: The Report
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Jonah files his official report: weather event, records incomplete, no actionable findings — then resigns his commission, unable to keep serving an institution that would call Wren's grandfather a criminal and Tam an accomplice. Emotional beat: a man trading career for conscience.

chapters.title: Last Train Before the Last Night
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. With the truth settled, Jonah packs to leave — his posting ended, nothing keeping him. At the station platform Wren almost says stay, and doesn't; he boards. She walks home along the seawall hating her own caution. Emotional beat: the blurb's promise inverted — the train leaves without her stopping it.

chapters.title: The Chapter She Couldn't Write
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Back at the lighthouse, Wren rereads her unfinished novel and realizes every ending she's written is a wall against this exact moment. She takes the manuscript, the letter, and her grandfather's restored logbook, and drives for the festival's final night. Emotional beat: fear converted into motion.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Jonah and Wren's POV, converging. On the festival's closing night, under the lantern release, Wren finds Jonah still there — he never boarded a connection; he'd been waiting to see if she'd come. She tells him the light stays lit whether or not anyone's watching, and so will she. First kiss in eleven years. Emotional beat: climax of the heart; staying chosen openly.

chapters.title: Elodie and the Letters
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, epilogue. Spring: the memorial stone stands, Tam's boat carries the crew's names, Maren and Wren bake for the season's first festival committee meeting. Wren finishes her novel — titled Elodie and the Letters — and dedicates it to 'the ones who stayed.' Jonah's coat hangs by her door. Emotional beat: resolution; love in the present tense at last.
